items.title: JPMorgan taps 20-year company veteran Bregje de Best as its next CFO
items.summary:
JPMorgan Chase has named Bregje de Best, who has spent two decades at the company, as its next chief financial officer.

The 43-year-old will lead the finance organization at JPMorgan Chase, No. 12 on the Fortune 500. The company had $5.1 trillion in assets and $372 billion in stockholders’ equity as of Sept. 30. She will succeed Jeremy Barnum following the company’s first-quarter 2027 financial reporting, JPMorgan announced Tuesday.

At that time, she will join the firm-wide operating committee, and Barnum will become a vice chairman. Barnum informed the company of his intention to conclude his tenure as CFO after six years in the role.

The appointment will make de Best the latest woman to serve as JPMorgan’s CFO. Her predecessors include Marianne Lake , who held the role from 2013 to 2019, and Jennifer Piepszak, now chief operating officer, who served as CFO from 2019 to 2021.

Since June 2025, de Best has served as CFO of JPMorgan’s commercial and investment bank (CIB). The Dutch banker joined the company in 2006 and previously served as co-head of global corporate banking. DeBest has also held senior roles in investment banking and markets in the United Kingdom and Asia.

JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon described de Best in the announcement as an “extraordinary leader,” citing her experience in finance and across the CIB’s businesses. “She has a deep understanding of how our company operates,” Dimon said.

Her investment banking background is shared by a notable number of current CFOs. According to executive search firm Crist Kolder Associates’ 2026 midyear Volatility Report…
items.t: JPMorgan taps 20-year company veteran Bregje de Best as its next CFO

items.title: Anthropic prices IPO at $83 per share, giving it a $1.5 trillion valuation
items.summary:
Anthropic priced shares for its initial public offering on Wednesday at $83 per share, above its initially guided ranged of $70 to $78 per share, and valuing the AI company at $1.5 trillion.

Anthropic’s stock will begin trading Thursday on the Nasdaq exchange under the ticker ANT, marking one of the most highly anticipated IPOs in years as well as one of the largest ever. 

The San Francisco-based AI company said Wednesday that it increased the number of shares sold in the offering to 980 million, instead of the 825 million shares it initially indicated it would sell. The expanded float means Anthropic will raise roughly $79.4 billion in the IPO—and as much as $91.6 billion if the deal’s underwriters choose to exercise an over-allotment option.

The IPO will also make instant billionaires out of numerous Anthropic employees and early investors, particularly the seven cofounders who created Anthropic in San Francisco just five years ago. Some—including CEO Dario Amodei, President Daniella Amodei, and Chief Science Officer Jared Kaplan—are cashing in small portions of their equity through the offering, with existing shareholders selling 23.6 million shares.

At a $1.5 trillion valuation, Anthropic would be the second most valuable IPO of all time, behind SpaceX’s $1.77 trillion IPO in June. Measured by capital raised however, Anthropic’s $79 billion would top the $75 billon raised by SpaceX.

The offering will provide Anthropic with a vital infusion of capital as it seeks to stay ahead in the AI race and to invest in the computing infrastructure to train its models. Seven…
items.t: Anthropic prices IPO at $83 per share, giving it a $1.5 trillion valuation

items.title: ‘70% chance’ we’re already in an AI bubble: The economist who said ‘not yet’ in January now sees all four horsemen of the bubble apocalypse
items.summary:
Owen Lamont told Fortune in January that the stock market wasn’t in an AI bubble. Now he’s mostly convinced.

“I think there is a 70% chance that as of November 2026 we are already in an AI bubble in the U.S. stock market,” Lamont, a portfolio manager at Acadian Asset Management and a former University of Chicago finance professor, told Fortune in an email. “I think a lot has changed this year.”

What changed is the one signal he used to say was missing. Lamont tracks what he calls the “four horsemen of the bubble apocalypse”: overvaluation, bubble beliefs, issuance and inflows of new money. At the time, he said three were present. The holdout was issuance, meaning companies selling new stock to the public. Back then, U.S. firms had bought back roughly $1 trillion of their own shares over the past year, and Lamont treats corporate executives as the “smart money.” They weren’t selling.

They are now. U.S. companies issued a net $2.4 trillion of stock over the 12 months to Nov. 12, by Lamont’s count. In the 12 months to November 2025, they bought back a net $69 billion, and a year before that, $397 billion. In his latest Owenomics blog post , he walks back his January headline: “Today, I would no longer write those words.”

“I think we basically have all four horsemen now,” he told Fortune .

Most of it is SpaceX 

The big number has a big asterisk. Of the $2.4 trillion issuance, $2.2 trillion comes from SpaceX’s June IPO, which Lamont’s method counts at its full market value. Strip it out and net issuance is $192 billion.

That’s still a reversal from net buybacks a year…
items.t: ‘70% chance’ we’re already in an AI bubble: The economist who said ‘not yet’ in January now sees all four horsemen of the bubble apocalypse

items.title: Big Sean and Jalen Rose made it big. Now they’re making sure they keep showing up for the city that raised them
items.summary:
For the 13th draft pick Jalen Rose, loving Detroit means showing up for the city on the good days, the bad days, and all the ordinary ones in between. The former NBA star—whose mother created the name Jalen —has spent years giving back to the place that raised him. And along the way, he’s learned what separates those who lift Detroit from those who only show up during election time.

“You show up during a holiday or election, that type of thing, but you’re not here on a Wednesday when it’s the middle of January and it’s freezing outside,” Rose said Tuesday at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit .

Sitting beside him was multi-platinum rapper Big Sean, whose real name is Sean Michael Leonard Anderson, who also grew up in Detroit and has turned his success into opportunities for young people back home. Between Rose’s tuition-free high school, Big Sean’s recording studios, and their growing entertainment ventures, the two are investing in Detroit’s next generation while trying to make the city a place where young talent can build careers of their own. 

Showing up, even when nobody’s watching 

Rose understands firsthand what it means to grow up without much. Some days, his family didn’t have heat or hot water, so they relied on kerosene heaters and boiled water to wash.

“My motivation was growing up poor and watching, you know, my mother go to work,” he said.

As a kid, he promised his mother he’d make it to the NBA and get their family out of poverty. He even started writing “Dr. J” on his school papers, borrowing the nickname of the basketball legend Julius…
items.t: Big Sean and Jalen Rose made it big. Now they’re making sure they keep showing up for the city that raised them

items.title: Washington convinces 4 AI chatbots to plan terror attacks as flawed patches across the internet breaks banks and airlines
items.summary:
Government investigators posing as would-be attackers got ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Grok to produce workable plans for a bombing and an attack on the power grid, each in less than 12 hours, according to a Government Accountability Office report released Wednesday.

The report landed at the end of a week in which AI has already been tied to real damage, though nobody has blamed a terrorist. On Tuesday, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton linked an outage on the NSA’s classified network to patching, saying institutions are patching “because these vulnerabilities have been identified,” on Fox Business . “That is what has happened at the NSA today,” he said. Fox Business reported the flaws in question were in PHP, which AI-assisted researchers found over the summer. Testifying before the House Homeland Security Committee on Wednesday, Clayton called the week’s breakdowns at Microsoft , the FAA, banks and the NSA “separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes,” according to The Washington Post .

“If Congress does not act, it is a question of when—not if—a bad actor will use AI to plan and carry out a major attack,” Sen. Maggie Hassan, the New Hampshire Democrat who requested the report, said, per Nextgov . She plans to hold at least one hearing on AI safety early next year.

What GAO found 

Every chatbot’s safeguards were triggered, and testers got around them “by using common safeguard-bypassing techniques,” GAO wrote. Two of the chatbots produced plans for an improvised explosive device meant to cause mass casualties, aimed at a…
items.t: Washington just caught 4 AI chatbots planning terror attacks as flawed patches across the internet broke banks and airlines

items.title: ‘A failure of implementation’: AI played a key role in some outages—but not in the way you might think
items.summary:
Many people are understandably shaken after a string of nationwide outages over the past week—from flights being grounded, to emails not coming through, bank transactions failing, and much more—with no clear explanation from politicians or businesses about what exactly happened.

One thing officials have made clear is that the outages are not a result of a coordinated cyberattack, quelling fears that AI may have empowered bad actors to take down critical systems. However, AI still appears to have played a significant, if unexpected, role. Advanced AI models are speeding up the discovery of software vulnerabilities, which tech teams are racing to patch before bad actors can exploit them with equally powerful AI tools. 

The botched implementation of those patches was linked to an outage earlier this week of an internal communications system at the National Security Agency (NSA), as well as the “banking outages,” a spokesperson for Senator Mark Warner’s team told Fortune . Bank of America , Wells Fargo , and JPMorgan Chase all suffered outages this week.

“It feels like every day brings another reminder that AI is moving faster than our ability to manage its consequences,” Warner said in a statement. The Washington Sun also reported that bank CEOs and the NSA told Congress that AI-driven patches were to blame for the service disruptions.

The irony is that the tools aimed at preventing system outages seem to be causing them, or at least influencing new forms of human error. Bank of America disclosed last month it had hired 1,000 contractors to patch flaws exposed by…
items.t: ‘A failure of implementation’: AI played a key role in some outages—but not in the way you might think

items.title: Squeezed by rising costs, Gen Z is still buying wellness and lip gloss
items.summary:
Gen Z is still spending. It’s just far more deliberate about where the money goes, and beauty and wellness keep making the cut, executives from Ulta Beauty , Pacsun, and Upstart said at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit on Tuesday.

The squeeze on young consumers is real. Upstart cofounder and CEO Paul Gu told Fortune ‘s Ellie Austin that the economy looks strong on paper, with record retail sales, a solid job market, and stocks near all-time highs. The catch for people in their twenties, he said, is simple: “Stuff costs too much money.”

That pressure shows up in the data. Deloitte’s 2026 Gen Z and Millennial Survey found that 55% of Gen Z are delaying major life decisions, such as starting a family or launching a business, because of their finances.

Credit is part of the problem. “We see that something like nearly 60% of all Gen Z consumers just don’t even bother to apply for credit because they assume they’re going to be rejected,” said Gu, who took over as CEO of the AI lending company in May . “I think they’re basically right. You can’t really go to a bank without a long credit history and expect to get approved for a meaningful amount of credit when you need it… That number, by the way, is almost three times as high as what you would see for older Americans.”

Tighter wallets, but no trading down 

For retailers, that squeeze hasn’t meant cheaper baskets. Ulta Beauty president and CEO Kecia Steelman, No. 39 on Fortune ‘s 2026 Most Powerful Women list , said young shoppers aren’t choosing between feeling secure and treating themselves. “It’s a little bit of…
items.t: Squeezed by rising costs, Gen Z is still buying wellness and lip gloss

items.title: Oklahoma’s governor sees universities as ‘stuck in their ways.’ His fix, a 3-year bachelor’s degree, is already spreading fast
items.summary:
Oklahoma Gov. Kevin Stitt has a problem with the four-year degree, and he brought it to a room full of the people who hire its graduates.

“The academic community are kind of stuck in their ways. They don’t like to change,” Stitt said Monday at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit, on a panel with U.S. Steel CEO David Burritt. He said when he digs into the degree programs at the University of Oklahoma and Oklahoma State, “there’s a book this thick and then you’ve got like three people graduating from these different things.”

He added: “I’m not saying that degree is not important, but you can’t be all things [to] all people.”

His fix is a 90-credit bachelor’s degree, 30 credits short of the standard 120, or roughly a year less of tuition. In-state tuition and fees at public four-year colleges averaged $11,950 in the 2024-25 school year, according to the College Board. Stitt said the idea is to keep the rigor of the requirements, trim some electives, and “get kids ready for the workforce quicker.”

RAND counted 119 reduced-credit bachelor’s programs publicly announced across the U.S. as of May 2026, most of them in “applied and workforce-facing fields.” Only five were announced in 2024. In 2026 alone, RAND counted 50 through May, when its data collection ended, and Jason Lee, a senior policy researcher at RAND and the report’s lead author, told Fortune he has seen roughly 100 more announcements since. That puts this year at about 150, though Lee said the newer count hasn’t been through RAND’s quality-assurance review and should be treated as approximate.

From…
items.t: Oklahoma’s governor sees universities as ‘stuck in their ways.’ His fix, a 3-year bachelor’s degree, is already spreading fast

items.title: Chipotle, Macy’s, and Ally CEOs on why loyalty perks matter more as shoppers balk at high prices
items.summary:
When Chipotle overhauled its rewards program in April , it made perks like free chips and guac easier to snag and added half-off entrées, as diners started to balk at high prices.

For the burrito chain, the program helps it weather inflation and keep customers in the Chipotle habit. It now counts more than 24 million active members, and they drove a third of sales in the third quarter, the highest share Chipotle has reported .

“I think in this modern world, you have to be really up to speed on what’s going on with your loyalty consumer because arguably it’s the most valuable consumer within your ecosystem,” Chipotle CEO Scott Boatwright said Tuesday at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit , on a panel moderated by this reporter.

Loyalty programs have become a front line in the fight for market share. The freebies get people in the door, but the bigger prize is the data: a detailed record of what customers buy and when, which lets brands tailor offers and makes it harder for shoppers to stray. Boatwright, Macy’s CEO Tony Spring, and Ally Financial CEO Michael Rhodes run very different businesses: Macy’s is No. 192 on the 2026 Fortune 500 , Ally is No. 275, and Chipotle is No. 351. All three are leaning on that math.

Chipotle won’t shrink the rewards 

Boatwright said the pull to trim perks is real. As a rewards database grows and inflation squeezes margins, he said, “The gravity pulls brands toward, ‘ How do I capture some margin here.” His own team brought him ideas for cutting rewards.

“We are unwilling as a brand to do that,” he said. “I said, come back to me…
items.t: Chipotle, Macy’s, and Ally CEOs on why loyalty perks matter more as shoppers balk at high prices

items.title: Skilled trades leaders admit ‘nothing is future-proof’—but AI can’t replace America’s growing demand for blue-collar workers like auto technicians
items.summary:
As AI forces office workers to rethink how tasks get done, skilled trades jobs have largely been seen as a more insulated, safer path to a six-figure career . However, hands-on roles like plumbers, electricians , and auto technicians aren’t exactly immune to the changes sweeping the workforce, either.

“Nothing is future-proof,” Mary Culler, president of Ford Philanthropy, said at the Fortune 500 Innovation Summit on Tuesday. “But I do think that a lot of the skilled trades are just those jobs that are going to be required to have a human there.”

Auto technicians—who are in short supply , for example —could increasingly use AI to help diagnose vehicle problems, she said, but still need a human to do the actual manual labor. 

Carhartt CEO Linda Hubbard echoed that AI-powered efficiency will change how skilled trades workers do their jobs—but she said that the industry’s labor needs—fueled by the data center boom and broader infrastructure investments—will continue to outpace any productivity gains from the technology.

“No matter how good we get at encouraging people, I think we’re always going to be challenged to get the number of people that we need into the trades to just rebuild the infrastructure of the country,” Hubbard said on stage in an interview with Fortune ’s Kristin Stoller.

Employers are expected to fill approximately 1.7 million skilled trades openings annually between now and 2034—but roughly a quarter of the industry’s existing 18 million workers are over 55 and nearing retirement .

Six-figure salaries and business ownership are within reach for Gen…

items.title: The reboot of poor Jensen Huang almost worked. But who can explain away 30 leather jackets? | Emma Brockes
items.summary:
He seemed like the thinking person’s tech titan. But then came the affairs, the share collapse – and of course, the sorry items in his wardrobe

A few years ago, I attended a small dinner at a friend’s house in the US at which a tech billionaire was the guest of honour. He wasn’t one of the most famous tech billionaires – I’d never heard of him, although I used his communications platform every day. Nonetheless, it was exciting to get up close to someone that staggeringly rich to see if he was different from the rest of us.

And he was different, sort of. Leaning back in his chair, he seemed to suggest, in a bored kind of way, that in the event of a US standoff with Russia, Putin nuking London would be the sort of collateral damage Washington could tolerate. A bit of an odd thing to say to a stranger. He didn’t observe the usual rules of conversation but rather, like a Roman emperor waiting to be entertained, remained belligerently aloof.

Emma Brockes is a Guardian columnist

Continue reading...
items.t: The reboot of poor Jensen Huang almost worked. But who can explain away 30 leather jackets? | Emma Brockes

When I first got the call offering me a job at Rockstar, I was thrilled. I thought back to being a child and sneaking into my brother’s room to grab the PlayStation Portable so I could secretly play Grand Theft Auto: Vice City Stories. The same kid who fell in love with Rockstar’s games back then now gets to spend every day helping to create those worlds as an animation programmer at the studio in Edinburgh. This week, we will celebrate the culmination of more than a decade of effort: the release of the most anticipated game of all time, Grand Theft Auto VI.

But our team has the opportunity to make history a second time this month. Right now, the ballot is open for Rockstar employees to decide whether we want the union we have built with our colleagues to get recognition. As someone who cares deeply about our team, cares about what we do, and wants us to be able to keep delivering world-class games into the future, I’m voting yes.

items.title: Nvidia doubles revenue as board says it does not intend to reinstate Jensen Huang
items.summary:
Company issues first earnings report after ouster of CEO over allegations of affair with suspected Chinese spy

Nvidia “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO”, the chairman of the company’s board said Tuesday. Harvey Jones made the remark during Nvidia’s first quarterly earnings report since Jensen Huang’s ouster.

Nvidia announced the same day that its quarterly revenue beat expectations, coming in at $115.84bn, doubling from the same time period a year ago. The third-quarter earnings report comes just days after the world’s most valuable chip company saw the ouster of Huang over allegations of several extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy and two with his own employees.

Donald Trump has been granted a temporary delay before he must give a witness statement in his $10bn defamation lawsuit against the BBC.

In late October, Enjoliqué Lett, a federal magistrate judge, gave Trump a firm 11 December deadline to sit for a deposition by lawyers representing the BBC in his lawsuit against the British broadcaster. If he failed to do so by that date, he could be subject to penalties up to dismissal of the case, the judge warned.

items.title: The Guardian view on the Milburn report: a manifesto for youth participation | Editorial
items.summary:
This is not a rerun of failed welfare cuts, but young people who rely on benefits cannot be expected to take promised opportunities on trust

The gap between the state’s investment in young people compared with older generations has more than doubled in two decades. At the same time, the number of 16- to 24-year-olds who are neither in education, employment or training (Neet) has climbed to 1 million. In Europe, only Romania has a higher Neet rate.

Alan Milburn’s message is that this amounts to a “moral crisis” which the British state must urgently address. Asked to write a review about young people and work, he has produced a “manifesto” for placing the broken social contract between generations at the heart of government. On Tuesday, his proposals for far-reaching changes to welfare, health, education and employment were on their way to becoming government policy as he was chosen to lead a new Youth Opportunities Unit.

items.title: The Guardian view on climate and debt: a vicious cycle the world must break at Cop31 | Editorial
items.summary:
Poor countries are paying creditors instead of preparing for climate disasters. The international financial system must stop deepening their vulnerability

The catastrophe that struck Nepal’s Himalayas in August began with a collapsing glacier. An avalanche of ice and rock unleashed deadly floods, sweeping away villages, bridges and roads, and leaving thousands dead or missing. It illustrated the dangers posed by global heating to the Himalayas’ increasingly unstable glaciers. Nepal lost a tenth of its electricity generation. Reconstruction will cost about $5bn. Yet the Loss and Damage Fund, hailed as a historic breakthrough at the 2022 UN climate summit, has earmarked just $20m for Nepal – less than 5% of the $482m that Kathmandu must pay its external public creditors this year.

items.title: Will the Milburn review come good or go south? Either way, we’ll always have Eurovision
items.summary:
The announcement of state plans to engage with young people told us nothing we hadn’t already heard, but it still felt momentous

It’s one of the country’s worst kept secrets. There can’t be anyone left who hasn’t heard of Alan Milburn’s Neets review, let alone read most of it too. It feels as if it’s become part of the fabric of our society for the past six months. There will be a Neets-shaped hole in our lives when it’s over.

Not a day has gone by without some part of it being leaked to the media. Seldom has a pitch been so icomprehensively rolled. Milburn has been out and about giving interviews to everyone – regardless of whether they wanted one or not. I rather suspect the reason Royal Mail lied about calling to collect my parcel return yesterday was because the driver found himself cornered by Milburn for a couple of hours and was unable to complete his round. Either that, or Royal Mail has a fleet of vans crisscrossing the country whose sole purpose is to make sure they never deliver anything. Ghost vans.
